+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 18 June, Malta rider ([profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/24499098/overview]) messaged Bolt CS in-app ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/594161879]) complaining about being “_recorded without permission_”.
** The rider took a trip with a driver who had an internal dashcam. Apparently “_He had no sticker warning signs showing he has a camera viewing the inside of the car_”. The rider claims “_According to gpdr law no one can takr a video of someone else without permission_” (this is not correct).
* CS responded noting the following:
** “_Drivers are not Bolt’s employees and are designated as independent data controllers under the respective privacy regulations. This underlines their responsibility to ensure the alignment of any CCTV camera use with the local laws of the country where they operate_” - this is _mostly_ correct.
** “_we have requested Muhammad to provide the Privacy Notice outlining how personal data from the CCTV are being processed and taken necessary steps to enhance their compliance when setting the CCTV in the car by offering guidance for adhering to the regulations_” - It is a shame that CS specified the driver by name. CS ticket to the driver is [here|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/594438318] - thankfully, this only makes _recommendations_ and so does not appear to create reclass risk. Driver has not responded.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Similar issue to [+LSS-48754+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-48754]. CS has gone slightly further than we would ordinarily go, but otherwise taken the correct approach.
* The only outstanding issue is that the rider is waiting for details of the driver’s privacy notice / data processing activities, which the driver has not provided. It is unfortunate that CS promised this.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* In any case, we should tell CS not to over-promise driver privacy notices going forward.
* If driver responds, then we can review and provide some reassurances to the rider.
* If driver does not respond, we should send the following:

_Dear Joanna,_

_As noted in previous messages, please note that we passed on your concerns to the driver and reminded them to keep in mind their privacy obligations, including with regards to transparency. However, since drivers are independent service providers, and therefore are independent data controllers, it is up for them to assess whether their use of a dashcam acts in line with applicable privacy laws. We are therefore unable to take any additional steps at this time - however, if you have any questions, please let us know._

_Yours sincerely,_

*_Bolt_*

* As a general comment going forward, while it is correct to say that drivers are independent service providers / data controllers, we should avoid promising riders that we will ask the driver for a copy of the driver’s privacy notice. This is unnecessary and can result in us promising something that we are unable to deliver on.

h1. Delivery Pricing Performance and Endpoint Optimisations

* *June 29, 2023*: Enabled gzip compression on Redis cache entries to reduce payload size by ~70%, cutting Redis network I/O by an estimated 50–80%. Compression added minimal CPU overhead (<10%) and resulted in significantly lower memory and bandwidth usage on the Delivery Pricing Redis.
* *November 29, 2023:* Enabled *automatic scaling (HPA)* for the Delivery Pricing Eater service in production, so that the service dynamically adjusts pod count based on demand. This Horizontal Pod Autoscaling optimisation significantly improved resource utilisation and cut hosting costs by about *50%* while maintaining performance. (Before autoscaling, the service cost a constant $9.7/day; after, it scaled down during low traffic to ~$34/week total, roughly half the previous cost.)
* *March 22, 2024:* Introduced a new *caching mechanism for courier routes* in the pricing system. When a courier is assigned a batch of orders, the chosen route is now cached for *2 hours* (configurable). Reusing the same route data for the final earnings calculation ensures the courier’s final payout closely matches the initial proposal and avoids recalculating distances for that order batch. This backend change improves consistency and reduces duplicate work in the earnings computation pipeline.
* *June 14, 2024:* Implemented proactive *cache invalidation* for delivery fees when campaign-based discounts expire or are invalidated. Previously, delivery fee results were cached for 30 minutes, which could lead to stale prices if a discount ended. The new logic keeps the same ~30 min TTL per fee but will *invalidate and refresh the cached fee entry early if a relevant Campaign changes* (expiry or fraud disablement). This was achieved by extending shared library code (NodeJS Common) to support targeted cache eviction, and it required an upgrade of the Redis backend (from v6 to v7) in production to deploy these changes. The result is more *up-to-date pricing* for users with minimal performance impact.
* *August 30, 2024:* Removed an unnecessary performance-tracking decorator ({{timedAsync}}) from the pricing code to *reduce event-loop lag*. This decorator was originally used for measuring performance metrics, but it introduced overhead on each request. After eliminating it, the *event loop lag* in the service dropped by ~40% (from a ~1.9 ms maximum down to ~1.1–1.3 ms), and average request durations decreased slightly (by about 40 ms). This change streamlined the backend execution path, yielding a small yet measurable improvement in response latency.
* *October 4, 2024:* Deployed multiple related optimisations to pricing endpoints and data flows. A *new internal endpoint* {{/internal/getPricingDataForProvider}} was introduced in the Delivery Provider service to return provider pricing metadata entirely from a *cached source* (using the providers metadata cache). This means Delivery Pricing no longer calls a live provider service for each fee calculation, and instead quickly fetches provider settings from cache, greatly speeding up retrieval of provider configuration data. In tandem with this, all Delivery Pricing Eater endpoints were updated to send only provider *IDs* (rather than full Provider objects) in requests, since the necessary provider details are now fetched via the new cached endpoint. This streamlined the request payloads and eliminated redundant data fetching across services. _Additionally_, the team *replaced calls to the Delivery Zone Definition service with in-memory data* for zone lookups within pricing. The prior implementation was hitting an external {{/internal/zones/listByLocation}} API for each fee computation, which had begun showing high latency (~2 s response) under heavy load (~20k requests/minute). Now, zone information is loaded and *served from memory* in the pricing services, drastically reducing those external calls. This change (applied to both pricing-eater and pricing-courier services) improved fee calculation times and reduced cross-service traffic caused by zone lookups.
* *October 11, 2024:* Implemented a *two-layer caching system* for provider pricing data. Previously, all provider pricing configs were cached only in *Redis* (remote cache). Now, an in-process *in-memory cache* serves as the first layer, with Redis as a secondary fallback cache. This layered cache (using a new {{LayeredDataRepository}}) keeps the most frequently used data in-memory for ultra-fast access, while still leveraging Redis for distribution and longer persistence. After deploying this update to production, the team observed a *dramatic drop in Redis network I/O* – from over 30 MB/sec down to under 1 MB/sec – since most requests are now satisfied in-memory. Memory usage per pod did increase modestly due to the in-memory storage, but remained well within acceptable limits. Overall, this change reduced latency (by avoiding network calls to Redis for hot data) and alleviated load on the caching infrastructure.
* *November 15, 2024:* Migrated the primary Delivery Pricing database (for the courier pricing service) from a traditional MySQL instance to a *TiDB cluster* to improve query performance. The migration was completed smoothly with no issues, and it immediately resulted in *faster response times across all database queries* in the delivery-pricing-courier service. This backend change (moving to TiDB, a distributed SQL database) improved the throughput and latency of pricing calculations that rely on database reads/writes, benefiting overall response times for those endpoints.
* *March 21, 2025:* *Deprecated an old internal endpoint* that was causing unnecessary load. After Eater apps migrated to a new Geo-based distance service, the team removed the legacy {{/internal/getRouteDistanceFromProvidersToEater}} endpoint (which Pricing had owned) from use. Retiring this endpoint and fully switching to the new Delivery Geo service for distance calculations *streamlined the codebase and cut down ~10k requests per minute* that were hitting the pricing service during peak times. This deprecation reduced redundant work in the pricing backend and improved overall system throughput.
* *May 23, 2025:* Completed a major overhaul to speed up delivery fee calculations when requesting fees for many providers at once. A suite of improvements were rolled out across multiple services and endpoints:
** A new *v2 pricing data endpoint* on the Provider service ({{/internal/v2/getPricingDataForProviders}}) was introduced to serve provider pricing info entirely from cache, eliminating slow lookups and ensuring data is fetched efficiently. The previously used provider data endpoint was removed in favor of this cached solution.
** On the pricing side, the Delivery Pricing Eater service got new *batch-oriented endpoints* that accept full provider objects (including traits, location, etc.) directly, so that the Pricing service doesn’t need to make separate calls to Provider for those details. These changes cut down cross-service chatter and were designed to *reduce latency* in fee computations. All consumer services (provider search, eater analytics, basket, etc.) were updated to use the new endpoints, and the old ones were retired.
** Several *internal code optimisations* were made in the Pricing Eater service: replacing the heavy Lodash library functions with lighter alternatives (e.g. using {{fast-deep-equal}} and custom clone functions for objects), and *parallelising* various calls that were previously sequential. For example, fetching prerequisite data (targeting configs, provider-specific overrides, dynamic multipliers, route distances, etc.) is now done in parallel, and database queries are run in parallel with cache reads wherever possible.
** These improvements yielded dramatic performance gains. For high-volume endpoints like {{getDeliveryFeeForProviders}}, the *99th-percentile latency* dropped significantly: in one analysis, the team saw response times go from ~2.35 seconds down to <400 ms (~5× improvement) for an analytics service calling this API, and from ~500 ms down to ~250 ms (~2× improvement) for provider-search service calls. Overall, the *average fee computation time* across services fell from ~600 ms to ~200 ms (~3× faster) after deployment. This allowed the team to increase the batch size – they went from handling 200 providers per request to *1,000 providers per request* – while still keeping response time under 300 ms. These enhancements in caching, endpoint design, and parallel processing vastly improved the throughput and responsiveness of delivery pricing calculations at scale. Each environment (staging and production) was closely monitored during rollout, and a performance dashboard was set up to track these latency improvements.

Are these questions posed by the client and our answers correct?

+*Q.:*+ Regarding the data controller status — you mentioned that you are the data controller. Please justify this by specifying the legal basis under which you assume this role (e.g., legal obligation). Is there a legal act or an explanation from the State Data Protection Inspectorate on this matter? According to the provisions of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) 2016/679, EDPS guidelines, and considering the purpose — that you are acting in our interests and on our behalf as the data controller — we believe your status, in the context of our agreement, should be that of a data processor.

+*A.:*+ _As mentioned previously, please note that Bolt acts as an independent data controller when providing services to business customers. This role is clearly set out in Section 4 of the Bolt Business General Terms and Conditions (_[_link_|https://bolt.eu/lt-lt/legal/]_), which explicitly states that Bolt and the business customer act as separate and independent controllers with respect to their respective processing of personal data._

_Bolt determines the purposes and means of processing personal data required to operate the platform, manage user profiles, optimize transportation logistics, and ensure safety and compliance. In doing so, Bolt assumes full responsibility for its own processing operations and ensures full compliance with applicable data protection laws, including the GDPR._

_In support of this classification, Guidelines 07/2020 of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB) on the concepts of controller and processor under the GDPR provide authoritative guidance. In particular, paragraph 82 and the "Example: Taxi Service" on page 27 illustrate a situation where a digital platform independently determines the processing of user data in connection with transport services. Although Bolt is a ride-hailing platform and not a taxi operator, the example provides useful analogical reasoning. IIt supports the conclusion that platforms which operate the digital infrastructure, determine user experience and data processing objectives, and contract directly with customers typically qualify as data controllers._

_Furthermore, as per Article 4(7) of the GDPR, a "controller" is the natural or legal person that “alone or jointly with others, determines the purposes and means of the processing of personal data.” Bolt determines why and how it processes personal data related to drivers and business accounts — from user registration, location tracking, fraud prevention, and invoicing — thus meeting the definition of a controller._

_To further demonstrate Bolt’s commitment to data protection, the company holds ISO/IEC 27001 certification, an internationally recognized standard for information security management. This reflects that Bolt not only assumes the role of a data controller in a formal sense but also implements a high level of operational and technical safeguards to protect personal data in accordance with Articles 24 and 32 GDPR (responsibility of the controller and security of processing)._

_In conclusion, both the contractual terms and the actual nature of Bolt’s data processing activities support the position that Bolt operates as an independent controller. This role is consistent with GDPR definitions, EDPB guidance, and applicable legal standards. Therefore, each party — Bolt and the business customer — remains independently responsible for their respective compliance obligations, including the provision of privacy notices, legal bases for processing, and the exercise of data subject rights._

Hi [~accountid:5b7bea09d08e47445d6fd01e] , re-posting the privacy assessment:

🔴 *Advice: DO NOT LAUNCH in Portugal without consent.* We must delay launch until consent functionality is implemented. Launching without this would violate Portuguese criminal law and privacy law.

We cannot legally launch the audio trip recording feature in Portugal without first obtaining prior consent from _all_ parties recorded, including non-Bolt users who may be captured (e.g. third parties in the vehicle).

*Legal analysis*
Following consultation with external Portuguese counsel, key risks and requirements are as follows:

# *Consent is mandatory*
#* Under the Portuguese Criminal Code (Art. 199), it is a criminal offense to record private conversations without the express consent of _all_ participants.
#* Constitutional protections (Articles 26 and 34) reinforce the privacy of private communications.
#* ePrivacy Law requires prior and express consent for recording oral communications unless specific legal exemptions apply (none apply to Bolt’s use case).
# *GDPR + Local law compliance*
#* Legal basis for audio recording = GDPR Article 6(1)(a) (consent)
#** Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous.
#** Consent is required before recording begins, including for _non-users_ (e.g. friends or family riding along).
# *Risk exposure*
#* Very high risk of enforcement or criminal liability if recording starts without valid consent.
#* Although the DPA is not very active, public complaints (from drivers, riders, or competitors) could trigger serious repercussions.
# *Additional requirements*
#* Clear privacy notices must be provided to all impacted individuals.
#* Retention should not exceed 30 days, with automatic deletion within 48h post-retention unless tied to a criminal proceeding.
#* App functionality must be adapted to collect valid consent before any recording starts.

Hi [~accountid:712020:0f7a089b-3b06-423b-844c-6e5ac370aa1e] - we’ve performed a Red Flag Review of Docebo’s DPA and unfortunately there are some issues that I would recommend we address.

I have shortlisted these for you below. 

We will need additional time to propose amendments to their DPA to address these risks - by tomorrow morning. However, I am concerned that there won’t be enough time to negotiate these with Docebo. Let me know how you’d like to proceed?

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
h4. 1. *No Processor Indemnity & Liability Cap (Clause 13)*

*Risk:* Docebo provides no indemnity for personal data breaches and limits its liability under the general commercial cap in the main agreement.
*Why It Matters:* If Docebo causes a breach or regulatory issue, Bolt may bear unrecoverable financial and reputational consequences.
*Action:* Request a specific processor indemnity and either uncapped liability or a higher, separate cap for DPA-related claims.

----

h4. 2. *Reuse of Personal Data for AI by Default (Clause 2.5)*

*Risk:* Docebo may use Bolt data (in anonymised and aggregated form) for AI development unless Bolt opts out.
*Why It Matters:* Anonymisation methods aren’t detailed, raising re-identification and regulatory risk.
*Action:* Opt out by default; amend the clause to prohibit reuse without explicit, written consent and safeguards.

----

h4. 3. *Uncontrolled Third-Party Access via End Users (Clause 2.9)*

*Risk:* End Users may enable third-party integrations that bypass sub-processor and data transfer safeguards.
*Why It Matters:* This could expose personal data to unvetted third parties without proper controls.
*Action:* Audit platform permissions; restrict end-user capability to activate third-party access.

----

h4. 4. *International Data Transfers Without Approval (Clause 10)*

*Risk:* Docebo may process data globally—including in high-risk jurisdictions—without Bolt’s prior approval.
*Why It Matters:* Bolt cannot assess data transfer risks or compliance exposure in advance.
*Action:* Require notification for new processing locations, a list of countries used, and confirmation of safeguards.

----

h4. 5. *Unverified Technical & Organisational Measures (Clause 5 & Annex A) - FYI* [~accountid:6061907490e3950069a3a5d3] 

*Risk:* Docebo applies its own security standards without confirmation they meet Bolt’s expectations.
*Why It Matters:* Insufficient technical measures could leave Bolt liable for preventable breaches.
*Action:* Have InfoSec review Annex A; ensure measures meet Bolt’s InfoSec Code of Practice. Push for InfoSec Code of Practice to apply as a baseline standard.
{panel}

As per the Section 9 of the Agreement, the Agreement is valid until *31 December 2025*.

Under the same section of the Agreement, the ordinary termination of the Agreement during its term is excluded. The rights of the partners to extraordinary termination for good cause in accordance with § 314 of the Civil Code of Germany remain unaffected. Good cause shall be deemed to exist in particular if:

* a partner repeatedly or seriously breaches the confidentiality agreed in § 16 of the Agreement,
* the respective contributions agreed between the partners in this cooperation agreement are not made in the intended scope and period or the provisions of this agreement are otherwise violated in a serious and repeated manner.

Pursuant to the above terms of the Agreement, we have no right to terminate the agreement for convenience. The Agreement can only be terminated subject to existence of a good cause in accordance with the terms of the Agreement and Clause 314 of the Civil Code of Germany. As usual, a good cause for termination shall be duly proved and well grounded by the terminating party, otherwise there is a high risk of a dispute. 

As far as I understand from the information provided in this ticket, you wish to terminate your cooperation in the municipality of Kleinmachnow. Is my understanding correct that you are also cooperating under the Agreement in other areas of Germany and Kleinmachnow is one of them? If this is the case, there is an option to approach the BVG asking to terminate the cooperation under the Agreement only with respect to Kleinmachnow municipality avoiding termination of the Agreement in its entirety. In any case, please note that the Agreement does not specify the procedure for partial termination of the Agreement thus it would be subject to mutual negotiations. 

Hope this helps, but please let me know if you have any questions or a clarification is needed. Thank you!

+*BACKGROUND*+

* On 25 June 2025, French rider ([profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/identity/consumers/rider/260595099/overview]) wrote to Bolt CS in-app ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/598741028]) complaining about use of internal dashcam (also general complaint about the driver being late - nothing for us to address there).
** NB. This was initially escalated as a personal data incident - it is not.
* CS responded with the following:
** “_Drivers are not Bolt employees and are designated as independent data controllers under the respective privacy regulations. This emphasises their responsibility to ensure that any use of CCTV cameras complies with the local laws of the country in which they operate_” - This is correct. (/) 
** “_Bolt has taken the initiative to request privacy notices from drivers to inform you about how CCTV data is processed, ensuring transparency and a clear understanding of how your personal data is managed_” - Unsure why we are offering this, as this places unnecessary obligations on us. Not a compliance point; just odd ⚠️ 
* CS messaged driver ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/598714089]) asking for PN. 
** Appears to be based on this KB article: [Link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/kb/articles/internal/78437?country=global&language=en]
* Driver responded “_I do indeed have a dash cam that is visible. … I would also like to inform you that I do not keep any recordings of my customers. On the contrary, it is intended for the safety of my customers and myself in case of any problems_”.
* CS wants to know how to proceed.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* Similar to [+LSS-52441+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-52441]. It seems that CS are not by default reliant on the KB article. The article is not _wrong_, but it is creating unnecessary effort on our part, and messaging drivers about our “_concern_” towards dashcams is misleading.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Recommend that going forward we should not ask drivers for PNs, and guidance should be updated accordingly.
* For the present case, we can respond to the rider with the following, in light of the driver’s confirmation.

_Dear Blandine,_

_We passed on your concerns regarding the internal dashcam to the driver and reminded them to keep in mind their privacy obligations, including with regards to transparency. The driver has confirmed that they do not keep any recordings of passengers taken on this dashcam, which is primarily intended for safety purposes. We hope that this addresses your concerns._

_As noted in previous messages, since drivers are independent data controllers with regards to the recordings collected on internal dashcams, it is up for them to assess whether their use of a dashcam acts in line with applicable privacy laws. If you have any additional questions, please let us know._

_Yours sincerely,_

*_Bolt_*

Hi [~accountid:712020:c6829626-18d0-4d73-9974-74d1569b4bdf] , 

Thanks for the proposal but amounts are not reasonable based on the Bolt Travel policy and daily allowance guideline [https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/FIN/pages/4421519012/Daily+allowances+and+other+travel-related+costs|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/FIN/pages/4421519012/Daily+allowances+and+other+travel-related+costs|smart-link] We should try to operate with the general €50 or max €75 unless there is a need to have higher rates based on the legislation. The reference you did to the local law CAO Rijk – Tarieflijst buitenlandse dienstreizen (per 1 jan 2025) is actually a document which includes *maximum* rates for accommodation, meals, and incidental costs per country—used by *Dutch government ministries*.  There is no reason to have those max rates for Bolt employees, just to think what is reasonable to have.  I have used AI to investigate more about rules in NL. It was confirmed that private employers *are not required* to use these CAO Rijk amounts—they can use *lower fixed rates,* reimburse *actual expense or* mix both (e.g. hotel on actuals, meals on per diem).

I couldn’t find proposal for amounts in case of domestic travel. I have found the following guideline for NL:

*Lower Daily Allowances – Common in Private Sector*

Many companies (especially SMEs or those with tighter travel budgets) adopt *lower daily rates*, such as:

||Type of Expense||Common Private Sector Rate||
|Breakfast|€8–10|
|Lunch|€10–12|
|Dinner|€20–25|
|Incidental costs|€5–10|
|*Total per day*|*€40–55*|

As for international travel, could you think about simplified approach for international travel daily allowances? It’s possible in NL to set reasonable flate rate:

h3. Summary of Dutch Practice – International Per Diems

||Approach||Tax-Free?||Documentation Needed||Common In||
|CAO Rijk Tariff (per country)|✅ Yes|No (if used as fixed)|Government, NGOs, larger firms|
|Custom Flat Daily Rate|✅ Yes|No (if reasonable)|SMEs, tech, consulting|
|Actual Expense (Receipts)|✅ Yes|Yes|Corporates, travel-intensive firms|

Hi [~accountid:5fc110f331795a006f947e12],

Based on Bolt’s T&C (5.9, 6, 7.6, 7.10, and 13.6), I do not identify any significant legal risks that would prevent the implementation of the proposed model, provided that merchants are properly informed in advance and given a reasonable opportunity to opt out. 

I believe it is important to ensure the following safeguards:

# Merchants should be notified of the feature *in advance*, accompanied by clear and sufficient explanations, including what the feature does, why it improves system reliability, that it does not affect who gets paid or how refunds are processed, and any other relevant context.
# Merchants should be given a reasonable timeframe during which *they can opt out of the feature if they choose*.
# We can include a disclaimer, such as: “This change applies only to retail locations that are legally and technically capable of accepting cash payments (e.g., operational fiscal cash register). If you are unable to support such payments, you may opt out via the provided link.”



Additionally, it would be important to clarify how you intend to introduce this new feature/requirement. Specifically, will this require an update to the Terms and Conditions? Or will it be treated as a functional/app update that does not require a formal T&C amendment?



‼️ It should also be noted that this payment model would not be permissible for alcohol purchases in Latvia. Under applicable law, *cash payments are not allowed for online purchases of alcohol*; only non-cash payments are permitted in online retail involving alcoholic beverages.‼️ 



Finally, have you considered resolving this issue by targeting drivers couriers? If you have not yet considered this option and would be interested in that, please let know and I could look into the legal possibilities.

If you have any other questions - let me know!

[~accountid:712020:6ec9ea6b-f071-41dc-ab0a-54910568f43d], from a legal perspective, there are two available options to extend the contractual relationship:

a) the first and more efficient option is to execute an addendum (or annex) to the existing agreement, extending its term of validity fro 12 months, i. e. until 11 June 2026. This approach has been adopted in the current situation, with the addendum specifying that it shall enter into force and be binding on the parties as of 11 June 2025, thereby ensuring there is no gap in the agreement’s continuity or enforceability;

b) the second option would be to re-execute the agreement in its entirety, entering into a new contract with a validity period extending through 11 June 2026. From a legal and practical standpoint, this option is generally less favorable. It may require additional time for negotiation, as the counterparty may insist on a thorough review of the entire agreement and seek to renegotiate certain terms, regardless of whether changes were intended. This could introduce unnecessary delays and the risk of reopening settled terms.

# Switch call from including {{categories=""}} to {{categories"accommodation"}}
# Remove street and number comparison between venue layer and address layer responses

Comments: We applied both changes listed above and noticed during manual testing that accommodation venue was getting prioritized over a certain area. The area was wide enough to actually still display the venue name across the street. To avoid causing such a user experience we decided to implement 1 and keep 2 as is.

As part of this change we tested multiple cases:

# Switch call from including {{categories=""}} to {{categories"accommodation"}} and remove street and number comparison between venue layer and address layer responses *→* Venues get prioritised and sometimes we see venue even if we are acorss the street
# Switch call from including {{categories=""}} to {{categories"accommodation"}} and keep street and number comparison between venue layer and address layer responses *→* Restricts venues so that we may still get address response even if the pin is over a hotel for example
# Keep {{categories=""}} and remove street and number comparison between venue layer and address layer responses *→* No improvement
# Switch call from including {{categories=""}} to {{categories"accommodation"}} and calculate linear distance for address / venue reverse geo and pick the closest to the request’s coordinates *→* Did bring an improvement, some hotels that were tested were no longer displayed if the pin was on the other side of the street. However, moved around the map on multiple venues and did not conclude this change is actually a fix with minor misses. Thus, decided to not proceed further.

# *How will incident or safety reports be handled?* (Do we have a flow for complaints that originate with third-party services?)
# *What’s the expected rider experience if a trip is cancelled or something goes wrong?* (Do we message that clearly in the app?)

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*BACKGROUND*
{panel}

* AKI’s investigation stems from a driver’s compliant about an inadequate DSAR response (see [+DSR-529+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/DSR-529]).
** Concerns a a Lithuanian driver ([profile|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fleet/drivers/edit/6278629?tab=profile&filter=%7B%22limit%22%3A25%2C%22offset%22%3A0%2C%22filter%22%3A%7B%7D%7D&tz=Europe%2FTallinn]), whose account and payouts have been suspended.
*** Based on internal investigation, this relates to suspicious payout activity on certain Bolt trips during April 2025.
**** Tag “_BAD_PAYMENT_RIDE_” applies to the rides, as well as “_Payout id [197085444] was suspicious and flagged_”.
**** Based on comments on the SD ticket: “_The driver demonstrated signs of_ +*_systematic failed payment fraud_*+_. From the onset of the suspicious activity, fraudulent orders accounted for approximately 50% of his earnings_”.
***** _“All orders were roughly the same distance, with similar routes and multiple destination changes, allowing to maximise the price with minimal pre-auth requirement. All orders were done systematically, at roughly the same times and always back-to-back. Also, if you take a look at the associated user accounts, trips with this driver were typically the last trips so far on their account. Therefore hinting towards a planned failed payment fraud, on individual rider accounts - after which the rider accounts were discarded.”_
***** _“Additionally many of the failed payments were due to “first used” or “restricted” error, which can hint towards stolen cards. BAD_PAYMENT_RIDE flag was applied automatically when there is a failed payment. The second comment you see about the flagged payout, was detected automatically by us due to the failed payments, and therefore suspended the payout. After which I manually reviewed the fraud orders. Again, we’d wish to be relatively vague when discussing fraud patterns_.”
**** The manual payout review, order review, behaviour analysis, refund decision and hard-block was done by Fraud Team.
*** Driver was informed on 28 April that their account was suspended due to ‘suspicious activity’ ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/563547381]). In particular, “_a number of orders were detected in your account that did not comply with Bolt's rules, which led to your account being suspended permanently_”.
** On 28 April 2025, the driver sent the following +*DSAR*+ to Bolt, via email ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/563669949]):
*** “_I respectfully request a detailed explanation of the specific reasons and evidence which led to the permanent suspension of my driver account, as per my rights under GDPR Article 15 and Article 22 regarding automated decision-making. Additionally, I hereby request a manual review of the decision made against my account._” As such, driver is asking for:
**** *(i) Explanation of why their account was suspended.*
**** *(ii) Supporting evidence re account suspension.*
**** *(iii) Confirmation whether the suspension was based solely on automated processing (this also applies to withholding of payment)*
**** *(iv) Manual review of these decisions.*
*** CS responses to the DSAR were unfortunately quite high-level, which led to further escalation:
**** “_your account was suspended due to irregular activities. You can find more information_ [_here_|https://bolt.eu/en/marketing-campaign-terms/general-campaign-terms-drivers/].” (2 May, [+link+|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/564059387])
**** “_the requirements outlined in the General Campaign Terms for Drivers also apply to your case, as they are not limited to campaigns only_.” (2 May, [+link+|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/564059387])
*** This led to the driver also requesting the following:
**** *(v) “**_All personal data held by Bolt related to my driver account and payment activity_**”*
**** *(vi) “**_Any internal system flags, risk triggers, notes, or logs used to justify the suspension or payout recalculation_**”*
**** *(vii) “**_A clear explanation of what is meant by “irregular activities,” including which specific trips or actions were involved_**.”*
** DSAR was formally acknowledged on 13 May ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/570767884]).
*** Unfortunately, it appears that no extension letter was submitted for this one. Instead, the language that was sent was just “_we are writing to confirm your request remains a priority among our teams and we are committed to providing you with a comprehensive response as soon as possible_”.
**** TBC with the contractor team why our usual extension language was not used.
** Therefore, at the time when the driver complained to AKI, the deadline was passed without a formal extension, and all that the driver had been told was that their account was suspended due to ‘suspicious activity’.
* On 26 June 2025, AKI sent the formal complaint to Bolt ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/599211764]).
** AKI flags that the driver alleges they have only received “_general answers_” from Bolt to date. AKI therefore asks for the following by {color:#ff5630}*7 July 2025*{color}:
*** {color:#4c9aff}*(1) “*{color}{color:#4c9aff}*_reply to the complainant's request of 28.04.2025 and provide specific explanations regarding the processing of his data”_*{color}
*** {color:#4c9aff}*(2) “*{color}{color:#4c9aff}*_send a copy of your reply to …_* {color}[{color:#4c9aff}*_info@aki.ee_*{color}|mailto:.info@aki.ee]{color:#4c9aff}*_”_*{color}
* The full response to the driver’s DSAR was sent on 26 June, minutes after we received the email from AKI ([link|https://beehive.bolt.eu/customer_support/case/570767884]). The response follows the approach we currently adopt for suspended account cases. It did the following:
** (a) Confirmed that the suspicious activity concerned “_repeated unusual order patterns and payment-related issues, were detected during Bolt trips that you were involved in between 17 and 27 April 2025_”, and that “_we are unable to disclose further information about Bolt’s fraud detection and prevention triggers and processes, as disclosing confidential information regarding such triggers and processes may allow third parties to circumvent such processes and threaten the security of Bolt’s users_”.
** (b) Attached a summary of the relevant trips and attached redacted internal note.
** (c) Confirmed that the decision to suspend the account was reviewed manually.

{panel:bgColor=#eae6ff}
*ANALYSIS*
{panel}

* We have already responded substantively to the driver’s DSAR, which we can provide to AKI. Thankfully, the decision appears to be the result of human intervention, which de-risks this.
** Nevertheless, worth checking if there is any more data we can provide (in case any was missed), as the more we can send to the user before responding ti AKI, the stronger our position becomes.
* However, before doing so (and since we have time), we should probably do the following:
** (1) Check with Njord whether AKI is likely to have any major concerns with the response that was sent to the driver.
** (2) Consider providing a more detailed explanation on why the account was suspended to AKI, so as to bolster our position regarding suspending the driver.

Hi [~accountid:62615f256cb53d006a6a3fe1] 

I don’t see any reason to tax this fee any differently from the already existing business fees. So, in PT, if it’s a client on the reseller model, the business fee should have the local max rate VAT of 23%. If it’s the intermediary model, it should be charged from Bolt Ops EE VAT nr, 0% VAT R/C.

For PT, the main point to flag is that commission must not exceed 25%. Bolt currently pays a 5% tax on commission, calculated after netting demand and supply incentives.

If this project could result in fleets having negative recurring commissions, we may need to reassess the approach. That said, we can address this reactively if and when it arises.

Currently, Martech x Engineering are ironing out details on where to draw the line in terms of ownership. [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07RWE69G3Z/p1750857726049859|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C07RWE69G3Z/p1750857726049859|smart-link]

Dear *Szocsi,* 



*Data Subject Access Request – Response* 



Thank you for your data subject request, which was received by us on *27 May 2025.*



After conducting a diligent search for records relating to your access request, we have confirmed that we do process the personal data requested. Data protection law entitles individuals to a copy of their personal data within the search scope – that is personal data, which identifies them, or enables them to be identified from it as a living individual person. 



As you may be aware, the right of access under data protection law does not provide an individual with an absolute right of full access to any and all documents containing their personal data. For example, that right should not adversely affect the rights of others, including our trade secrets or intellectual property and in particular the copyright protecting the software. Furthermore, we must point out that if after careful analysis we conclude that our rights or rights of others prevail, we will not be able to provide you with access to certain documentation where an exemption applies.



We will share copies of the personal data we hold about *you* to which you are entitled. This includes:

* *Vehicles* 
* *Security* 
* *Order History*
* *Online Status History* 
* *Identity Verification* 
* *Dispatch preferences*
* *Consents*
* *Communications*
* *Blocks* 
* *Account and profile* 
* *Telemetry*
* *Rating/Comments*
* *Acceptance Rate*
* *Average Rating*

In relation to your payment information as a fleet driver, payments are not made directly to fleet drivers by Bolt; instead, they are processed through their respective fleets. To access such information, we recommend reaching out to your fleet for assistance. They will be able to provide you with the necessary information regarding your earnings and payment disbursement.

* The purposes for which we process personal data;
* The recipients or categories of recipients to whom the personal data has been or will be disclosed;

* The sources of personal data received from other parties;
* Your rights in relation to your personal data;

* Details of any transfer of your personal data to third countries or international organisations and the safeguards used for any such transfers.

We appreciate your patience and understanding, and remain committed to addressing your request thoroughly and transparently. 

*Your rights* 



In addition to your right to access any personal data we hold about you, you have the right to request us to rectify, erase your personal data, restrict the processing of your personal data or to object to such processing. Any such requests that are received will be considered in conjunction with the applicable provisions of relevant data protection laws. 



If you are dissatisfied with this response to your request or in relation to any other matter relating to the processing of your personal data, we hope you will continue to work with us to resolve them. You also have the right to complain directly to your data protection/supervisory authority and, depending on the applicable data protection laws in your country, to seek a judicial remedy.

 

If you have any additional questions, please contact our Customer Support Team by replying to this email.

So Silja, here I am with some answer.
Here above, the query. it is the *same exact query* of last time.Some notes:

* pickup_expected_distance: this is the one generated at matching time, for that driver.
* dropoff_expected_distance: this is not the pricing distance. It is the one computed to update the ETAs, distances, routes on the agents screen.
** basically, the ETT/distance/routes updates. I took the one with the min. created date:
** so, that dropoff distance is the distance computed when the dropoff leg starts (ie, when the ride enters the ‘driving_with_client’ state)
* we could also have the pricing distance, but geo does not know which forecast will be picked by the pricing team (fastest? shortest?). So in this table there is not a way to discriminate btw the pricing dropoff-distance alternatives

Hey [~accountid:63abfbea7cde7bff9d78a2af], thank you for your reply. I do not understand the logic in your explanation. Since the courier should have tried to call the customer before contacting CS, aren’t we just repeating the same action that did not work for him?  The courier is attempting to contact the customer using the same phone number we have available in the ticket and admin. Therefore, it seems redundant for us to call the same number again.

Outgoing calls are a significant time consumer for CS, and in the above-described case scenario, it does not seem to bring the pros that would outweigh the cons.

Not to mention, the process seems several years outdated. We used to call the customer in every single such case years ago. Then the process was changed, which allowed the couriers to handle the situation without live CS assistance. Thanks to that change, the courier can leave the delivery area quicker, improving our supply. It also benefits our KPIs like CCPO and AHT.

Needless to say that the current (outdated) process is not future-proof for scaling. The more the market grows, the more prominent these issues become. And given which specific KPIs this negatively affects, it could potentially snowball into further issues during peak CS times (e.g., affecting other ticket response times).

I hope we can reach some common ground here and improve the process together.

Have a great day!

[~accountid:712020:13033e65-435c-4794-a380-e007eba7615a] 
1. Yes, the summary is accurate. The driver’s account was suspended due to a clear pattern of activity indicative of systematic failed payment fraud. The orders in question exhibited highly consistent behaviours: similar routes, closely timed back-to-back trips, not following the route points, and an unusually high volume of tips, all with failed payments.
2. Fraud orders can be found [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1-QjzQnSYbto9Lmb1GvcbR4JmAW6vVzeHfVTEY-C_Pus/edit?gid=0#gid=0] marked in red. All of these trips:

* Resulted in a failed payment
* Show patterns of route manipulation or unexplained detours
* Included significant tips
* Were performed in a repetitive, back-to-back manner

These indicators collectively suggest that the trips were structured to maximise earnings in a manner inconsistent with legitimate driver behaviour.

Sharing with the driver: We can confirm to the driver that the account was suspended following identification of a repeated pattern of failed payments and route anomalies across multiple trips.
Sharing with a regulator: Should a regulator request supporting evidence, I believe the flagged orders and technical payment failure details (including timestamps, route logs, and payment failure reasons) may be shared, as these are factual and verifiable data points supporting our decision. But ultimately this decision should be up to you.
3. The driver's payout was suspended and deleted → at which point he was not allowed to receive the payout, but his account balance remained the same. Afterwards, refunds for the fraud trips were made for a total of 529.60 EUR, placing his account balance to -108.57 EUR.
4. Yes, we are confident. The only automated component was a temporary payout suspension (up to 36 hours), which is a standard procedure that allows time for manual fraud review by a real person. All subsequent actions - including behaviour analysis, order review, refund decisions, and account suspension, were performed manually by a person.
5. While his reply appears well-formulated, the volume, consistency, and financial risk associated with the detected pattern of trips remain significant. The back-to-back structure, payment failures, and inflated earnings present a risk level that is too high to justify reinstatement. Therefore we recommend keeping the suspension on indefinitely. 
However, if a formal legal process requires the release of non-fraudulent funds, we support processing such a payout in line with regulatory obligations, while still keeping the account suspended from active operations.

{code:sql}WITH user_cancellations AS (
  SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', etl.created_date) AS month,
    etl.city_id,
    etl.user_id,
    COUNT(etl.order_id) AS cancelled_orders
  FROM ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders AS etl
  WHERE 1 = 1
  	and etl.created_date >= CAST(DATE_ADD('month', -3, CURRENT_DATE) AS DATE)
  	--and etl.created_date >= DATE_TRUNC('month', DATE '2025-03-01')
    --AND etl.created_date < DATE_TRUNC('month', DATE '2025-04-01')  -- or use current_date for dynamic
    AND etl.city_id IN (79, 169, 1688, 170)
    AND etl.order_state <> 'finished'
  GROUP BY
    DATE_TRUNC('month', etl.created_date),
    etl.city_id,
    etl.user_id)
SELECT
  month,
  city_id,
  AVG(cancelled_orders) AS avg_cancelled_orders_per_user,
  MAX(cancelled_orders) AS max_cancelled_orders_per_user
FROM user_cancellations
GROUP BY month, city_id
ORDER BY month, city_id{code}

Vendor refused our template → conducting red flag review of Vendor’s DPA



*Low risk:* Pseudonymized personal data (location: journey starting point and journey end point)

*Use case:* We’ll only use their service to draw locations on the map (user-related data is displayed separately and handled within Bolt application)

 

*Review here:* [https://docs.google.com/document/d/1b73cOAIPNWDkHjCaZ5DEfMXLabyJcAQ77wPwgsPGZxU/edit?tab=t.0|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1b73cOAIPNWDkHjCaZ5DEfMXLabyJcAQ77wPwgsPGZxU/edit?tab=t.0|smart-link] 



*Red flags*

🔴 *Engagement of sub-processors:* general authorization for MapBox to engage sub-processors who fulfill the standard of the DPA. Potential risk of unmonitored onward transfers → due to low-risk of data processed, pushing back only a bit to retain a sense of control over sub-processors.

🔴 *Audit:* limitation to once per year → changed to need / circumstance basis. If deficiencies found, Vendor shall bear the costs and must correct deficiencies. Removed “big 4” requirement on auditing firm.

🔴 *Notifications of personal data breaches:* Mapbox only commits to notifying “promptly” and may provide information in phases → suggested stricter requirements

🔴 *International data transfers:* Mapbox incorporates the EU SCCs (Modules 2 and 3) and refers to DPF (Data Privacy Framework) certifications. However, DPF does *not* replace the need for SCCs in high-risk processing. Overreliance on the DPF can be problematic, particularly after _Schrems II_ and pending evaluations of US data adequacy → adding additional safeguards in helping with TIA, etc. Due to low-risk processing, keeping adequacy decision.

The Selfie Check is used to prevent fraud and ensure safety of our platform, and is based on Bolt’s _legitimate interest_. The Selfie Check may be conducted either manually by a human agent or through facial recognition technology, depending on the user’s choice. If you choose to proceed with facial recognition, we will request your explicit consent, this is obtained when you click the “Confirm” button. Your biometric data obtained during the selfie check procedure, is processed to authenticate your account and to verify your identity. In case the courier is technically actually unable to initiate the call, then it makes perfect sense that they would reach out to CS, and CS would try to make the call in their stead.

But from what I understood, while we talked about this topic with our team, the issue with foreign numbers of customers is often not a technical issue, but rather that the courier might be charged by their service provider for calling the foreign number.

Which, while understandable, is not a good reason for the courier to delegate it through CS. It seems to me more like their own operating cost, similar to the cost of fuel or mobile internet services, which they are trying to avoid or bypass by asking us to make the call in their stead.

And if the courier were to contact CS claiming that they need us to call the customer because of technical difficulties, then it would make sense for CS to put notes in both profiles (customer and courier). That way, we would see in the future whether this is an issue with that customer’s specific phone number (if the common denominator is the client) or whether the courier is just trying to delegate these calls through CS to save money (if the common denominator is the courier).

In terms of the process, it would be simplified to a single process without any condition about the foreign number. Instead, in case the courier had any technical difficulties contacting the customer, CS would assist them by trying to contact the customer themselves and then adding relevant notes into both profiles.

1.There can be various reasons for the payment failures, but the focus is more on the overall pattern of events and how these ride-hailing orders were structured. The conclusion of potential fraud or card theft isn’t based on a single failure reason, but rather on the repetitive nature and context of the failed transactions. The idea of a stolen card is more of an informed assumption that arises when a broader bad payment pattern is detected.

2.We did initially withhold a payout, and afterward, refunds were issued from the driver’s existing balance. It's important to note that a driver’s balance functions as a pooled account, not a traceable ledger of individual transactions, so it's not possible to directly link specific earnings or deductions. The balance simply reflects the net position between income and any liabilities, such as refunds.

Hi Kirill,

Thank you for your requests relating to your Rider Rating, which we received on 2 June 2025. 

Your Rider Rating as it appears in your Bolt app is calculated as an average rating based on your ratings from the previous 365 days. Each rating is from 1 to 5, as provided by the driver at the end of each trip. Further information on Rider Ratings can be found here: [https://bolt.eu/en/rides/rating/|https://bolt.eu/en/rides/rating/]. Please note the following in this regard:

* We are not able to provide you with data that pertains to specific rider ratings that affect your average rating. Data protection law requires a data controller such as ourselves to protect the rights of third parties, and disclosure of the requested data would violate the rights and freedoms of the relevant driver that provided the rating.
* Ratings provided by drivers about you are inherently subjective and reflect the personal experience of the driver. As such, they cannot be considered factually inaccurate or strictly requiring correction without a compelling reason for doing so. 
* Similarly, Bolt collects individual ratings about you given by drivers to determine an average Rider Rating and both: (i) encourage positive, safe and respectful interactions between passengers and drivers on the Bolt Platform; and (ii) empower drivers to make informed decisions about accepting or declining ride requests. Bolt’s legitimate interests in enhancing safety, quality and trust on the Bolt platform is overriding in such circumstances, and as such we are unable to delete individual ratings without a compelling reason for doing so. 

We would like to assure that although 1-star ratings between drivers and passengers result in those users being unmatched for future trips, a single lower rating provided by a driver about you does not significantly affect your access to or use of the Bolt platform. For more information on how we process your personal data, please review our privacy notice: [https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides|https://bolt.eu/nl-nl/privacy/privacy-for-riders/?category=rides].

We hope this helps to address your concerns. Should you have any further questions or concerns, please do not hesitate to contact us.

Yours sincerely,

*Bolt*

*Legal Summary* 

From the legal side, there’s a difference between these two:



# Inflating prices before discounts:
## This is sketchy from a consumer protection view, even if the merchant shows the required “30 days lower price” (which is lower than the discounted price). We can block such vendors from campaigns or reduce their visibility - this is low risk. We can also send them emails, reminding them that artificially inflating pricing before applying discounts can be found as unfair commercial practice. :green: 



# *Higher prices on Bolt Food vs. in-store* are {color:#36b37e}*allowed*{color}. We *cannot contractually require price parity*, especially in markets where we have significant share (>30%). However, we _can_ take other action based on inflated prices:
##  *Low risk*  :green:: 
### Withholding co-funded campaigns from vendors with lower in-store prices. However, they should be able to run their own campaigns (where Bolt does not co-invest) without interruptions still. 
### Removing visibility from home category (e.g. {{inflated-prices}} tag) IF we are running a co-founded campaign and they inflate prices in the middle of the campaign. 
## *Moderate risk* :yellow_circle:  : 
### Removing visibility from home category (e.g. {{inflated-prices}} tag) IF we are +*NOT*+ running a co-founded campaign. This is riskier since we cannot justify the lower visibility by limiting Bolt’s campaign costs. Under P2B, we have to disclose to the merchants how we rank them and if we limit their visibility, we have to tell them why. If we cannot justify the lower ranking by “keeping campaign costs under control”, then removing visibility can be seen as enforcing a price parity clause (i.e. even if we don’t have a price parity clause in TCs, we “punish” merchants for it). 
## *High risk  (not recommended)* 🔴: 
### Increasing commission if they have higher in-store prices. This is again risky since this can be seen as “punishing” merchants for not having price parity. One-sided commission increases are sketchy already, we don’t want to add fuel to the fire by using it as a punishment method. 
### “Predatory pricing restaurants - We will add to their description that “Restaurant has inflated prices”. This will also drive eater attention to it. “  - this is not recommended, since having higher prices is not illegal. Even if there’s a Bolt (co)founded campaign, we should not use this, as there is nothing illegal about it.

When we limit driver to only be able to execute some specific task, the effect is three-fold:

# We are in better control of what they do. This helps to push drivers to tasks with higher priority, which is our ultimate goal
# If drivers do choose optimal routes, then restricting their choice will add overruns and can decrease their performance.
# At the same time, we don’t know how efficient is our navigation in comparison to their own navigation skills, so driver performance actually can change in any direction

*As for the metrics to track:*

# Our ultimate goal is to reduce GMV lost due to late battery swap. So the obvious metric would be “GMV lost due to late swap”. However, this metric is affected by multiple factors: weather, drivers’ headcount, vehicle supply, price, and of course, task navigation system. It will be super complicated to claim that change in “GMV lost due to late swap” is due to navigation system and not anything else. I propose to measure what we actually change (*% of tasks with high priority closed out of all tasks closed)* and also establish a relation between this metric and GMV.
# As this feature may add overruns and unpredictable impact drivers performance, I’d want to track *drivers performance (task closed within 8h shift*). It should not drop
# In analysis we include only cases when shift consists of swap tasks by at least 90% (a few other tasks are acceptable, but we do focus on swap shifts)

*Experiment design:*

# Traditional AB test is hard: first, drivers will definitely communicate and in the worst case scenario can even start using other driver’s account. We also can’t really randomize drivers like we can randomize users. There will definetely be differences in drivers’ performance and characteristics we can’t control for in case we have just a few drivers.
# I propose we go with a diff-in-diff approach, when we pick 5-10 markets, and keep some 5-10 markets with similar climatic and operational conditions as control. We’ll compare trends in key metrics in affected cities VS trends in key metrics in control cities.
# As this feature is a significant disruption to drivers’ work, I would suggest we go in steps: launch 1 city for a week, gather mostly qualitative feedback. If new flow does not have critical issues, launch the experiment in 5-10 markets

** Initial CS response was to say that we cannot do this for them, and they should do so themselves via the child’s account portal.

*** Full Name: Mariam Maisuradze

*** Phone number associated with the account: +49176 11119800
* This was unfortunately not escalated to me until 27 June.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* We have been asked to advise on the ‘Explore Your City’ campaign ([+link+|https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1PvPUNNp3usitKf-v8hXsISXb7nemzw46gSVOblmGaEM/edit?slide=id.g2c52ccba8de_0_1456#slide=id.g2c52ccba8de_0_1456]). Encourages users to explore cities using Bolt (e-scooter or car) by including ‘rewards’ at locations of interest.
** *Marketing campaign*
*** As part of this campaign, Bolt will be promoting an app (which powers the interactive map experience) developed by external technical partner, Adventure Lab.
*** Plan is to market the campaign “_through OOH, digital ads, and other communication channels_”, all directing users to our Bolt landing page.
**** Specifically: OOH, Adventure Lab app, digital ads, push notifications, in-app comms, emails, in-app slides, campaign webpage and social media.
*** Users will be informed that they need to download the Adventure Lab to access the map and participate in the challenge.
*** *Question* is “_Are we allowed to refer users from our own channels to a third-party app, as long as it’s clearly disclosed that the app is developed by an external partner?_”
** *Prize draw*
*** Once signed up, participants are encouraged to find at least one hidden location in their city (Stockholm, Oslo, or Helsinki) using the Adventure Lab app. Participant scans a QR code through the Adventure Lab app to receive the reward.
*** Anyone who finds at least one location will automatically be entered into a prize draw for a gift card (Bolt credits) worth approximately €500. One winner per country will be randomly selected from the app participants.
*** This information will be clearly communicated on our campaign landing page.
*** Apparently app does not share personal data with us. However, “_we will reach out to the selected winners through the app and request their email and phone number in order to award the prize_.”
*** *Question* “_Is this setup legally compliant with local lottery regulations in Sweden, Norway, and Finland? Are there any adjustments or disclaimers we should consider?_”

+*ANALYSIS*+

* *Overall risk:* {color:#36b37e}*Low*{color}
** Location element does not appear to involve live GPS data. Processing will be mostly within data subjects' expectations.
** Purposes / Legal Bases:
*** Marketing Bolt services and those of partners (consent and legitimate interest, depending on whether targeted - explicitly covered in privacy notice).
*** To facilitate the campaign with our partner (legitimate interest - *_not explicitly covered in privacy notice_*, but we could make arguments that it is in-scope).
** Since participants will be actively signing up to the campaign by downloading the Adventure Lab app, they are unlikely to be frustrated by the associated processing.
* *Marketing*:
** We are technically promoting the services of another company here, by encouraging Bolt users to download a third-party treasure hunt app. If such promotions are sent directly and by electronic means, then we will be caught by marketing rules, and consent would be needed.
*** Direct = Email, push notifications, in-app comms
*** Not direct = Banners, webpage, slides (if not targeted).
*** Also anything not sent by Bolt is out-of-scope.
** Opt-out registers:
*** Sweden: No national opt-out list specifically for email marketing. Applies to calls.
*** Norway: No national opt-out list specifically for email marketing. Applies to calls and post.
*** Finland: ASML (Finnish Direct Marketing Association) maintains a voluntary opt-out list (Robinson List), which includes email. Not a legal obligation, but best practice to respect consumer preferences here.
** We should always ensure the user can unsubscribe.
* *Prize Draw*:
** We should ensure that campaign T&Cs are entered into, so that it is clear how winners are selected. This would also cover any transparency gaps.
*** Sweden Marketing Act requires no misleading claims or unfair practices, and that there are clear T&Cs for participation and how winners are selected.
*** In Finland, the Consumer Protection Act and Marketing guidelines by Finnish Consumer Ombudsman require transparency on terms and value of the prize and not creating misleading impressions.
*** See Dreamhack example at [+LSS-41407+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-41407].
** NB. From a quick Google, to avoid lottery law regulations biting, we should ensure that participation is free of charge and skill is not a factor.
* *Data Sharing:*
** It seems likely that some Bolt user data will be shared between us and Adventure Lab here. However, the scope of the data sharing is ultimately unclear.
*** In order for Bolt to award the winners, presumably Adventure Lab would need to provide us with details of the winner… but this is unclear.
*** Also worth confirming controller / processor setup here.
* *Retention*:
** We want to ensure that the marketing team is aware that the data collected for this local campaign is not stored longer than needed - standard approach is the duration of the campaign, but not longer than a few months.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* *Questions*:
** What is the timeline on this?
** How long is the campaign for?
** Are we just talking about riders / e-scooter users?
** Is there any overarching agreement between Adventure Lab and Bolt already in place?
** Assuming that this will be a _Bolt_ campaign, is it governed by our standard campaign terms? This is for Legal to prepare.
** What data sharing is going on here? Which data, in what direction, and for what purpose? Which countries?
** What does OOH stand for?
** How exactly will we be marketing this to Bolt users?
** Any lottery law regulations here?
* *Advice*:
** Marketing: When targeting users, ensure that we only send comms to users that have consented. If not targeted, then fine without consent. In any case, provide an unsubscribe option.
** Prize draw: Advise the usual campaign T&Cs to be used.
** Data sharing: Depending on setup, prepare a data processing / sharing agreement.
** Retention: No longer than necessary.

Hey [~accountid:62a057c3352bf40068d0411f]! Answering your question here: 

* How often have we had CYC participant no-shows in 2025? How big of a problem is this, i.e. is it worthwhile spending time on it?

February - 40 calls booked - 5 no-shows
March - 98 calls booked - 17 no-shows
April - 96 calls booked - 22 no-shows
May - 69 calls booked - 14 no-shows
June - 49 calls booked - 7 no-shows

In my head this is something that is worth spending some time on. This might not seem critical or a huge issue at first glance but I believe if we fix this or at least try this overbooking out after analyzing the participant attendance data, CYC will be a program that is more reliable and will build more trust to the program among PMs as well. I am pretty sure that this will reduce ReOps workload a bit as well. For example, right now there’s only one call booked for PMs - if that participant doesn’t show up, it means we suddenly need to:
Find a new time slot that works for PMs
Find a new participant 
Reschedule on quite short notice (for example a PM was supposed to have a call today but there is a no-show and the only free time-slot they have is tomorrow)

But if we book two or more participants for a single slot, there’s a significantly better chance at least one shows up, ensuring the PM gets their weekly call without any delays and they can rely on having one single fixed time for their CYC schedule and hopefully no need to skip a week due to a no-show.

Hi everyone, I am re-opening this ticket considering the developments that took place in London over the past 7 months. [~accountid:63fe21787c30bbd6b33e09d3] please find all questions below

+*Strategy and Legal Grounds to Secure Borough MoUs for E-Bike Operations*+

*Summary:*
Requesting comprehensive legal guidance and support to develop a strategy and escalation plan to convince London Boroughs to sign Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) with Bolt for shared e-bike deployment.

----

*Background:*

* Bolt has been engaging with 17 London Boroughs for over 9 months to secure MoUs required to operate e-bikes in compliance with the TfL Code of Practice.
* Despite repeated engagement and submission of operational plans, most Boroughs have either indefinitely delayed or refused to sign MoUs, while allowing incumbent operators to operate under equivalent agreements.
* MoUs are operationally critical, as they permit use of Borough-managed parking bays and enable compliance with TfL expectations.
* Without MoUs, deployment carries significant legal, operational, and reputational risks (e.g., bike removal, fines, non-compliance with TfL).

----

*Key Questions for Legal Review and Support:*

1️⃣ *How can we best use legal arguments, escalation strategies, and formal correspondence to persuade Boroughs to sign MoUs with Bolt?*

2️⃣ *Explore the possibility and legal risk of launching operations in Boroughs without MoUs.*

* For example, sending a formal letter giving 30 days’ notice stating that we intend to launch absent engagement, and asserting that the Boroughs have a duty to cooperate or provide clear justification for refusal.
* Clarify whether such a letter creates any legal exposure, if it could be used against Bolt in enforcement, or whether it strengthens our position in subsequent challenges.

----

*Relevant Legal and Strategic Arguments to Develop and Deploy:*

h3. 1) Public Procurement Law – Equal Treatment and Transparency

* *Legal Basis:* Concession Contracts Regulations 2016
* If Boroughs grant access to parking bays (a valuable economic advantage) to other operators without transparent procurement, this likely constitutes an undeclared concession.
* Refusal or indefinite delay creates a procurement risk due to lack of transparency and unequal treatment of economic operators.

----

h3. 2) Competition Law – Abuse of Dominance and Market Foreclosure

* *Legal Basis:* Competition Act 1998 (Chapter II and potentially Chapter I prohibitions)
* Boroughs control essential infrastructure (public parking bays), placing them in a de facto dominant position.
* Selective denial of access creates discriminatory barriers to entry and restricts competition.
* This conduct could be challenged via a complaint to the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA).

----

h3. 3) Administrative Law – Procedural Unfairness and Unreasonableness

* *Legal Basis:* Common Law Principles of Public Law (Wednesbury unreasonableness)
* 9+ months of unexplained delay and lack of objective criteria or written decisions is procedurally unfair.
* Potential grounds for Judicial Review on the basis of unreasonable administrative conduct.

----

h3. 4) TfL Code of Practice – Engagement Requirements

* The Code expects Boroughs to engage constructively and agree operational plans.
* Refusal or delay is inconsistent with the Code and undermines pan-London regulatory expectations.

----

h3. 5) Proportionality – Lack of Justified Refusal

* Even if there are concerns, proportionality requires:
** Clear rationale.
** Opportunity for mitigation.
** A reasoned decision, not indefinite inaction.

----

h3. 6) Lack of Published Policy or Criteria

* No clear published criteria appear to govern decisions on which operators can sign MoUs.
* This strengthens the perception of arbitrary or discriminatory conduct.

----

*Requested Legal Deliverables:*
✅ Draft a formal pre-action letter to Boroughs citing:

* Procurement law risks.
* Competition law exposure.
* Procedural unfairness.
* TfL Code non-compliance.
* Policy inconsistency.
* A clear deadline for response (e.g., 30 days).

✅ Advise on the process and likelihood of success for:

* A CMA complaint.
* Procurement challenge under the Concession Contracts Regulations.
* Judicial Review for unreasonable delay.

✅ Explore the legal feasibility, risks, and implications of launching operations without an MoU after formal notice to Boroughs:

* Whether this strengthens Bolt’s position in any legal challenge.
* Whether it increases the risk of enforcement action or reputational damage.

Recommended wording if such notice is given.


*Deliverables to discuss together between Policy & Legal*

✅ Define a strategic escalation plan and precise language balancing firmness and constructive engagement.

✅ Define parallel engagement with TfL to demonstrate Bolt’s compliance and highlight Boroughs’ lack of cooperation.

# *OOH*: What does this acronym mean?
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
Subject to the answers to the above (_please confirm first_), my {color:#006644}*advice*{color} will likely look like the following:

* *Promotional Comms:*
** Where we are using *targeted* means (e.g., emails, push notifications, in-app comms) to encourage Bolt users to download the Adventure Lab app, we should only do so for users that have *consented* to receiving comms about third-party products and services. 
*** Where we are contacting Bolt users via untargeted means (e.g., banners and webpages, not at specific users / user categories), we do not need to obtain user consent.
** In the comms, we should: (i) make clear that the app is developed by an *external partner*; and (ii) always provide users with the option to *unsubscribe* from the comms.
* *Prize Draw:*
** Assuming this is a Bolt-led campaign, we should ensure that this campaign / the prize draw is *governed by clear terms and conditions* that set out how winners are selected, and which are *readily available* to participants. 
*** I defer to the Regional Legal Team  ([~accountid:712020:02e8ad5d-a35d-44b9-b445-6111cdb230dc] ) and the Marketing Team on what exactly these should look like, but I would expect it to look similar to the [+template terms+|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1__qFTQ22mX7zzAlds5OEeqjtYtVeeuEoyeUUrxA0koM/edit?tab=t.0] I have seen before. Once I have better visibility on the data processing elements, I can advise on the ‘Privacy’ section.
** I otherwise defer to the Regional Legal Team ([~accountid:712020:02e8ad5d-a35d-44b9-b445-6111cdb230dc] ) to consider local lottery regulations, as ths not not strictly a privacy law issue.
* *Data Sharing*:
** Depending on the Bolt user being shared with Adventure Lab here (or vice-versa), we may want to consider a *data sharing agreement* here to ensure that appropriate contractual protections are in place.
* *Retention*:
** To the extent that Bolt is specifically collecting any user data for the purposes of this campaign, it should be stored for no longer than is needed. The standard approach is the duration of the campaign, but not longer than a few months.
{panel}

+Why I wouldn’t remove it:+

* This incentivizes timely payments as it serves as a deterrent against delayed payments. Without it, there's less urgency for customers to settle invoices on time, which can disrupt Bolt’s cash flow and administrative efficiency, especially since Bolt acts as an intermediary collecting fees on behalf of third-party service providers.
* It covers real costs and risks. Late payments generate tangible costs for Bolt, such as administrative overhead, internal follow-up resources, and potential disruptions to remittances owed to service providers (e.g., drivers). Interest or late fees compensate for these indirect costs and risks.
* Imposing late payment fees is standard in B2B agreements to ensure fairness and financial discipline. Removing such clauses could set a precedent that weakens Bolt's contractual position with other clients.
